title: Hollow Square Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: four-way per-cell border checks versus classifying each row once and building it directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print an n by n square outline made of stars, the first row, last row, first column, and last column are all stars, while every interior cell is a space.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Picture Frame
blocks.text: Picture an empty picture frame lying flat on a table. Only the wooden frame itself, the outer edge, is solid, while the middle is completely open, showing nothing but empty space where a picture would normally sit.

blocks.caption: The border of the grid is stars, every interior cell is a space

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","*****","The first row is entirely border, since every cell in it is in row 0."],["Row 2","*   *","A middle row, only the first and last cells are border, the 3 cells between them are interior."],["Row 3","*   *","The same middle row shape repeats, since every non-border row looks identical."],["Row 4","*   *","Still a middle row, one row away from the last border row."],["Row 5","*****","The last row is entirely border, since every cell in it is in the final row."]]}

blocks.text: With only 2 rows, both of them are border rows, so there is no interior at all.
A single cell, which is on every border at once, so it is simply a single star.
This problem looks like it needs a per cell decision, but it is worth first asking how many genuinely different kinds of rows this shape can have.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Instead of asking "is this cell on the border" once per cell, a faster question to ask is "what kind of row is this" once per row, since every cell in a given row follows the exact same rule.

Observation 2: Testing a small example, n equal to 5, shows there are only ever two distinct row shapes here: the first and last rows are completely solid stars, and every row between them has a star, a gap of spaces, and a star.

Observation 3: Once a row is classified as border or middle, building it needs no per cell logic at all, a border row is just n stars repeated, and a middle row is a star, a gap of n minus 2 spaces, and a star.

Observation 4: And since only two distinct row shapes ever occur, no matter how large n is, both shapes can be built exactly once and reused for every matching row, then the whole pattern joined and printed in a single call.
That reframing, from a per cell question to a per row classification, is the single idea that turns four repeated border checks per cell into one decision per row.
Use two nested loops covering every row and column, and for each individual cell, check whether it lies on the first row, last row, first column, or last column.

items: Loop over each row and each column inside it.
For every cell, check if its row is the first or last row, or its column is the first or last column.
If so, print a star, since the cell is on the border.
Otherwise print a space, since the cell is on the interior.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check all four border conditions for every single cell

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: All four border conditions, first row, last row, first column, last column, are checked together in a single expression, for every one of the n squared cells, even though for most cells the row alone already decides the outcome.
The row loop and column loop are fully independent of each other, so no information about "what kind of row is this" is carried from one column to the next within the same row.
A single character, star or space, is printed per innermost iteration, keeping the per cell cost of this version fully visible.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every cell is individually tested against all four border conditions before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every one of the n squared cells requires its own four part condition check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking all four border conditions for every single cell is wasteful, since a cell only needs its row checked once to know what the entire row looks like, either every cell in it is a star, or only the first and last cell are. Deciding this once per row, instead of once per cell, avoids nearly all of that repeated checking.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every cell works but is wasteful: the same row-level fact, is this a border row or a middle row, gets tested n times, once per column, even though it only depends on the row index.

What is genuinely new here compared to the earlier pyramid problems: instead of a continuous formula giving a different length for every row, there are only ever two distinct row shapes, no matter how large n is.

What actually changes: the per cell border check gets replaced by a single per row classification, border or middle, decided once.

Can a known-length direct-construction technique still apply here: yes, once a row is classified, its shape, either solid stars or star-gap-star, is fully known and can be built directly in one or two operations.

The core idea: classify each row once as border or middle, then build that row directly instead of checking every one of its cells.

Classify each row just once: the first and last rows are entirely stars, while every other row is a single star, a gap of spaces, and a single star. Build that row directly with one or two operations, replacing n individual cell checks with a single row level decision.
For each row, decide once whether it is a border row or a middle row, then build that row directly and print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: decide the row type once, then build it directly

blocks.text: This works because a row's entire shape depends only on whether its row index is the first, the last, or neither, a single per row decision, and once that classification is made, the row content is fully determined; a direct repeat operation constructs a solid border row in one step, and concatenating a star, a gap, and a star constructs a middle row just as directly, with no dependence on checking individual columns.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A row's index is 0 or n minus 1","It is classified as a border row and built as n stars in one repeat operation","The row is correct immediately, with no per column checking"],["A row's index is neither 0 nor n minus 1","It is classified as a middle row and built by concatenating a star, an n minus 2 space gap, and a star","The row is correct immediately, and every middle row looks identical regardless of which one it is"]]}

items: The row classification, border versus middle, is decided once per row using the same condition that used to be checked per cell, but now it only runs n times total instead of n squared times.
A border row is built with a single repeat operation producing n stars, exactly the same direct-construction technique used for solid rows throughout this division.
A middle row is built by concatenating a star, a gap of n minus 2 spaces, and a star, three pieces assembled once instead of n individual per column decisions.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with only one row level decision per row instead of n per cell checks, and O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Since there are only ever two distinct row shapes, the border row and the middle row, both can be built once, reused for every matching row, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Build both row shapes once","border = \"*****\", middle = \"*   *\"","Since only two distinct row shapes ever occur, each needs to be constructed only a single time, no matter how large n is."],["Assemble all 5 rows","\"*****\", \"*   *\", \"*   *\", \"*   *\", \"*****\"","Every row simply reuses one of the two already-built shapes, according to its classification."],["Join and print once","The full pattern appears in one call","A single output call now produces the entire hollow square, regardless of how many rows it has."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reuse the two row shapes and output the whole pattern in one call

codes.python:
def hollow_square(n):
    top_or_bottom = "*" * n                     # the two border rows are identical
    middle = "*" + " " * (n - 2) + "*"            # every middle row is also identical
    rows = [top_or_bottom if i == 0 or i == n - 1 else middle for i in range(n)]
    print("\n".join(rows))                       # join every row and output the whole pattern at once


if __name__ == "__main__":
    hollow_square(5)

items: The border shape and the middle shape are each built exactly once, before any row assembly begins, since reusing them is possible precisely because only two distinct shapes ever occur.
Every row in the final list simply selects one of those two already-built shapes according to its classification, with no repeated construction work per row.
Joining all n selected rows with newline characters and printing once collapses the output down to a single call, regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: The key insight for hollow shapes is that most rows only take one of a very small number of distinct forms, here just two, a solid border row and a star-gap-star middle row. Once that classification is made per row instead of per cell, building the output becomes a handful of direct operations instead of a dense grid of individual checks.

items: Forgetting that the very first and last rows are completely solid, not star-gap-star like the middle rows.
Getting the middle row gap size wrong, it should be exactly n minus 2 spaces between the two border stars.
Not handling n = 1 or n = 2, where there is no interior at all and every row is a border row.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 1","A single star, since that one cell is on every border simultaneously."],["n = 2","Two solid rows of two stars each, with no interior row at all."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating the small number of distinct row shapes before writing any code, here just border rows and middle rows, is a strong signal of pattern recognition, and it directly leads to the row level optimization instead of a brute force per cell check.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how many distinct row shapes does this pattern actually have", think: name them explicitly before writing any code, here just border and middle.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every cell", think: classify the row once, then build it directly from that classification.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build each distinct row shape once, reuse it, join, print once.

items: Why does classifying rows into a small number of types scale better than checking every cell individually?
How would the row classification change if the shape needed a double thick border instead of a single thick one?
Can you extend this same row-classification approach to a hollow rectangle with a different width and height?
What is the total number of star characters printed, and how does it compare to a solid, filled square of the same size?
How would you adapt this approach if the border needed to use a different character than the interior fill?
The hollow pyramid, diamond, butterfly, and hourglass patterns later in this same division, which all reuse this same row-classification insight with different sets of row types.
The star and gap direct-construction technique from the earlier pyramid problems, reused here for the middle row shape.
Any grid problem where most cells share one of a small number of rules, checking a boundary condition once per row or column is faster than checking it per individual cell.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: four-way per cell checks in the brute force version, a single row-type decision per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: hollow shape printing, a new family in this division, where the key insight is not a continuous per row formula but classifying each row into one of a small, fixed number of distinct shapes.

Core Idea: every row is either a solid border row or a star-gap-star middle row, a classification made once per row instead of a border check made once per cell, so each row can be built directly, and since only two shapes ever occur, both can be built once and reused for every row.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: when a grid has only a small number of distinct row shapes, classify once per row rather than testing conditions once per cell.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with four nested conditions; naming the small number of distinct row shapes up front is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: only two row shapes ever exist here, border and middle, classify once per row and build directly.
